name: Giryama
confidence_why: Taylor 1891, Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1992 and Philippson's chapter in Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993 all place the prominent syllable on the penult, and the two modern sources agree that Giryama (Mijikenda) is a tone language with fixed penultimate prominence, differing only on whether that prominence is a metrical accent that attracts High tone (Cassimjee & Kisseberth) or predictable lengthening beside distinctive pitch (Philippson).

This is consistent with the catalog's fixed-penultimate coding (Taylor 1891's 'tonic accent on the last syllable but one') and refines it: the fixed penultimate prominence is predictable lengthening, not a stress accent, and the language is tonal — matching what the held Volk 2011 BLS paper says ('the penult is predictably lengthened'). It is a group-level (Mijikenda) statement read only as a snippet without a page number.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's fixed-penultimate coding (penultimate stress) and with the Nurse & Hinnebusch/Philippson statement that the penult is always prominent in Mijikenda. It adds the tonal side: the language has underlying H vs default L, and the penultimate prominence is analysed as metrical accent that attracts a pre-penultimate H, at word and phrase level. It is a group-level Mijikenda statement (Kigiryama is one of the nine languages covered; the worked examples focus on Chikauma and Chirihe).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mijikenda (nine languages including Kigiryama, abbreviated 'Gi') is a tone language: only High tones are underlyingly specified and other syllables get default Low. The penultimate syllable of the word is metrically prominent (an 'accent'), and a High tone located earlier in the word is attracted to that penultimate prominence ('Attraction-to-Accent'). The same rule applies at the phrasal level: 'if a word with a H tone in its underlying structure is followed by a toneless word, then the H of the first word will realign to the penultimate syllable of the second word' (p. 32). No stress independent of this fixed penultimate metrical prominence is described.
new_statements.exceptions: The authors ignore 'the complications that arise when more than one High tone appears underlyingly in a representation' (p. 29). Chidigo is singled out: the High attracted to the penult is not realized on the penult in the same way as in the other languages (the penultimate High 'shows up as such' only when the final syllable has a depressor onset, p. 30). Voiced oral obstruents act as depressor consonants and affect how the attracted High surfaces (fission of the H in Chikauma and Chirihe; other languages such as Chichonyi show only a High on the penult, pp. 31-35). Data are cited per language with tags Ch, Di, Du, Dz, Gi, Kam, Kau, Ra, Ri; Gi (Kigiryama) forms pattern with Ch and Ra in the present-tense paradigms on pp. 29-30.
new_statements.identity_note: Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1992 is a group-level Mijikenda statement covering nine languages (Chichonyi, Chidigo, Chiduruma, Chidzihana, Chikambe, Chikauma, Chirabai, Chirihe, Kigiryama); Kigiryama ('Gi') appears in the data sets, but the detailed argument is built on Chikauma and Chirihe, and Chidigo is noted as differing in how the penultimate High surfaces. Philippson 1991 covers East African Bantu generally (abstract names Kikuyu and Swahili as the endpoints).

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's fixed-penultimate coding from Taylor 1891 ('Tonic Accent.. on the last syllable but one'), but specifies its nature: the penultimate prominence is a demarcative LENGTH culmination, not pitch, and pitch (H tone) is distinctive and rule-governed (accentual/restricted tone system). This is the same account as the existing statement from Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993 (Philippson's prosody contribution: Mijikenda penult prominence 'due to length only, pitch contrasts being assigned distinctively') and is consistent with Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1992 (penult metrically prominent, attracts H). Taylor's exception (accent retracted to the root-initial syllable in certain tris…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Giryama (Mijikenda) has distinctive pitch: an 'accentual' (restricted-tone) system in which an H melody associates by rule to the penultimate syllable of the last foot (final syllable extrametrical; in Giryama 'c'est à la pénultième que s'associe le dernier H d'un syntagme, même dans les formes de surface', p.167). Independently of pitch, the penultimate syllable of the word carries a fixed demarcative accent realised as a culmination of LENGTH, not of pitch (Annexe rubric 10; ch.6 §3.5.2 type c, where Mijikenda is listed among 'langues à culmination de longueur, mais non de hauteur, sur la pénultième'). There is no surface vowel-length contrast, so penultimate lengthening is purely demarcative. Placement = penultimate, fixed; nature = length prominence in a language with distinctive H tones.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. The only other role of the penult given is metrical: in Shambaa, Bondei, Zigula and Mijikenda 'un pied ne peut être entièrement compris dans les limites d'un mot que s'il débute avant la more (structurelle) pénultième de ce mot' (p.484).
new_statements.exceptions: No exceptions to penultimate demarcative accent are given for Giryama. Philippson notes his Giryama data are limited ('Mes exemples giryama sont malheureusement en nombre limité', p.416 fn.2; post-lexical mechanisms not pursued 'faute de données', p.365); Meeussen's-rule rubrics 6-7 are marked '?' for Giryama. Digo differs from Giryama only in tone re-association (Digo re-associates H to the following/final syllable unless blocked by a voiced obstruent; Giryama re-associates once and never to the final), not in the penultimate accent (both 'accent démarcatif (culmination de longueur)').
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson treats Giryama as a dialect of Mijikenda ('dialecte giryama', p.364; 'giryama, autre parler mijikenda, très proche du digo', p.167), Sabaki group XVIII, Guthrie E72a; most of the detailed tonology in ch.4 §4.4 is Digo (after Kisseberth 1984) with Giryama compared; the Annexe gives Giryama its own summary entry. He states his Giryama examples are few.

tone_statements.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 2018. Why underlying representations? Journal of Linguistics 54(3): 591-610. Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/S0022226718000014 (Giryama: section 2, pp. 597-598, and (16b) p. 605; data from Volk 2007, 2011).
tone_statements.quote: In Giryama, a Mijikenda Bantu language of Kenya, the underlying rightmost /H/ is realized on the penultimate mora of the phonological phrase (Volk 2011: 17): (7) [...] In these examples, L tone is unmarked, while phrase-penultimate lengthening is indicated by doubling the vowel. As seen, the forms on the left consist of words and phrases that are all L tone (assigned by default). The forms on the right, on the other hand, have a H tone on the phrase-penultimate mora. It is quite clear that the only difference between the two sets of forms is the identity of the subject prefix: ni- ‘I’ vs. a- ‘he, she’.
tone_statements.locator: J. Linguistics 54(3), p. 597, section 2 'Why underlying representations?', around example (7); continuation p. 598 (examples 8-9, Ribe depressors) and p. 605 (16b) 'Giryama: /H/ shifts to penultimate position /á-na-mal-a/ → a-na-maála ‘s/he wants’'.
tone_statements.summary: Privative /H/ vs. zero (L by default); rightmost H realised on the phrase-penultimate (lengthened) mora = long-distance H shift; multiple Hs possible per phrase; in the Ribe dialect depressor consonants split one H into several surface Hs; penult prominence is length, tone is phonological not intonational.

readall_conflicts: No source places prominence anywhere but the penult. There is a difference of interpretation, not of placement: the Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993 passage (Philippson) says the always-prominent penult in Mijikenda owes its prominence 'to length only, pitch contrasts being assigned distinctively', whereas Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1992 treat the penult as 'metrically prominent' (an accent) that attracts a pre-penultimate High tone, at word and phrase level. Both agree the language is tonal (H vs default L) with a fixed penultimate prominence, so both are compatible with the catalog's fixed: penultimate syllable coding; they differ on whether to call that prominence accent or predictable length. Philippson's thesis abstract is silent on Giryama.

sources.citation: Hyman, Larry M. 2018. Why underlying representations? Journal of Linguistics 54(3): 591-610. Cambridge University Press. doi:10.1017/S0022226718000014 (Giryama: section 2, pp. 597-598, and (16b) p. 605; data from Volk 2007, 2011).

sources.quote: In Giryama, a Mijikenda Bantu language of Kenya, the underlying rightmost /H/ is realized on the penultimate mora of the phonological phrase (Volk 2011: 17): (7) [...] In these examples, L tone is unmarked, while phrase-penultimate lengthening is indicated by doubling the vowel. As seen, the forms on the left consist of words and phrases that are all L tone (assigned by default). The forms on the right, on the other hand, have a H tone on the phrase-penultimate mora. It is quite clear that the only difference between the two sets of forms is the identity of the subject prefix: ni- ‘I’ vs. a- ‘he, she’.
sources.locator: J. Linguistics 54(3), p. 597, section 2 'Why underlying representations?', around example (7); continuation p. 598 (examples 8-9, Ribe depressors) and p. 605 (16b) 'Giryama: /H/ shifts to penultimate position /á-na-mal-a/ → a-na-maála ‘s/he wants’'.
sources.note: Uses Giryama as a showcase of remote UR-surface tone relations: privative /H/ vs. zero; the rightmost underlying /H/ (e.g. of the 3sg subject prefix /a-/ or of a lexical verb root) surfaces on the penultimate mora of the phonological phrase, with phrase-penultimate lengthening; with two /H/s the verb-root H goes to the penult and the prefix H shifts one mora rightward; in Ribe a single /H/ yields several non-contiguous surface Hs before (non-prenasalised) voiced-obstruent depressor consonants; argues this is lexical/grammatical tone phonology, not phrasal pitch accent or intonation.

tone.quote: (1) Depressor consonants may “block” the spread or shift of a H tone to a targeted mora/syllable. (2) Depressor consonants may trigger surface forms with two or more non-contiguous High tones even though there is only one underlying H tone specification. … The insufficiency of this account will be demonstrated on the basis of Kigiryama. Specifically, we will show that H tone sometimes crosses a depressor and sometimes fails to cross a depressor. … the blocking and non-blocking effects of depressor consonants in Kigiryama …

Giryama based on Kisseberth's recordings; would state the penult-lengthening/prominence facts and their domain (phonological phrase vs word) directly, replacing an 1891 missionary sketch as deciding source and settling the word-domain field.

tone.quote: Underlying Tones e underlying opposition is of high vs. toneless. Verb stems may have an underlying high tone on the initial TBU, yielding two tonal types; for noun stems, a combination of a high tone on the initial and penultimate or ﬁnal TBU is possible, yielding six tonal types. … e last (or only) high tone in a phrase shis to the penult, e.g., Giryama a-na-mala ku-gula ŋgǔːwo ‘(s)he wants to buy clothes’. … Downstep When there are two adjacent surface high tones, most Mijikenda dialects have a downstep; however, this only happens on the penult.
tone.locator: Sect. 1.7 'Tone: An Overview', pp. 12-13; privative analysis restated ch. 2 intro p. 15 and Sect. 7.1 'The Basics of Mijikenda Tonology' p. 154; Giryama para Sect. 7.3 p. 163.

tone.summary: One tone, high, vs toneless, on morae of stems (verbs 2 types, nouns 6); the last H shifts to the phrase penult as a rise or fall; downstep on the penult; penult stress is length only.
